wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about their travel experiences. Each student writes three sentences: two true, one false about places they have visited. They share in pairs, and partners guess the lie. Teacher monitors for superlatives and present perfect.
wuAlt: Students complete the sentence 'The most amazing place I have ever been is...' and explain why. Teacher writes answers on the board.
Students interview a partner about their best and worst travel experiences using 'Have you ever...?' questions.
pres: Teacher shows a photo of Marrakech and a photo of Chefchaouen. Models: 'Marrakech has the most vibrant souks. Chefchaouen is not nearly as colorful as Marrakech.' Elicits superlative forms. Checks understanding with 'Which city is more crowded? Which is quieter?'
presAlt: Teacher uses a world map with pins. Students compare pinned destinations using 'as...as' and superlatives. Teacher corrects errors.
Teacher reads a short travel blog entry about Morocco and highlights superlatives. Students identify the structures.
prac: Students play 'Destination Duel' in pairs. Each pair gets two destination cards (e.g., Rabat vs. Casablanca). They must write five comparative sentences using superlatives and 'as...as'. Teacher provides a sentence frame: 'The best thing about... is... because...'.
pracAlt: Students complete a gap-fill worksheet with missing superlatives and articles. They then peer-check answers.
Teacher plays a 'Find Someone Who...' game where students ask 'Have you ever visited the most famous place in Morocco?' and tally responses.
ls: Students listen to a 2-minute audio of a traveler comparing two Moroccan cities (Fes vs. Essaouira). They fill in a table with 'best food', 'best weather', and 'best activities'. Teacher plays audio twice. Discusses answers to check comprehension of comparative language.
re: After break, students play 'Stand Up, Sit Down'. Teacher says a comparative sentence (e.g., 'If you think the Atlas Mountains are more beautiful than the Sahara, stand up'). Students stand or sit. Teacher checks for correct responses.
prod: Students choose two Moroccan destinations (e.g., Agadir vs. Tangier) and prepare a 3-minute pitch arguing which is the best. They must use at least three superlatives and two 'as...as' phrases. Pairs present, and class votes on the most convincing argument.
rw: Students read a short travel article about 'Top 5 Places to Visit in Morocco'. They highlight all superlatives and then write a 120-word email recommending one place to a friend, using the target language. Teacher circulates to check for accuracy.
st: Teacher shares a short personal anecdote about their favorite travel memory in Morocco, using present perfect and superlatives. Students share one travel story in groups. Close with: 'Today we compared destinations using superlatives. Thank you for sharing your experiences.'
g: Students race to write superlatives for categories (e.g., 'the most interesting city') on the board.
Students draw cards with adjectives and use them to compare two destinations in a minute.
Students look at two similar photos of Moroccan cities and write five comparative sentences.
Students create bingo cards with superlative phrases (e.g., 'the best food') and mark them off when classmates say them.
Students start a story with 'The most amazing thing I have ever seen in Morocco is...' and each adds a sentence.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a 50-word review of a Moroccan restaurant using superlatives.
Support learners: Use a sentence frame: 'The best thing about... is... because...' for their pitch.
hw: Write a 120-150 word blog post about your best trip to Morocco using superlatives and present perfect.
Record a 2-minute audio comparing two cities you have visited, using the target language.
Find a travel article about Morocco and rewrite it using five new superlatives.
tip: Encourage students to use local examples (e.g., 'The Hassan II Mosque is the most impressive building I have ever seen') to make language practice culturally relevant and meaningful.
